documents.title: Confidential settlement document: comparator analysis (Chandrasekaran conclusion; Albert Crenshaw)
documents.subject: Hamilton arbitration — analysis of pay comparators Chandrasekaran and Albert Crenshaw relative to Hamilton and Mayer across 1992-2002 salary snapshots
documents.notes: Page bearing the running header 'CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES / PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES'. A continuation page (starts mid-sentence), so at least one earlier page exists outside this batch. Not grouped with DOC-005, which is a different arbitration-procedures document.

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

two salary increases in 1998 in response to job offers he had received from competing newspapers.

Explanation
Chandrasekaran was considered one of the best reporters in Financial News. He covered both the technology beat for The Post and was the lead reporter covering the Microsoft Antitrust trial. At the same time, Chandrasekaran was The Post's lead Y2K reporter. By virtue of his excellent work and his ability to cover, simultaneously, these two important areas, Chandrasekaran was considered a highly-valued reporter.

Chandrasekaran received numerous job offers from competing newspapers and publications. In order to keep Chandrasekaran at The Post, Chandrasekaran was put on the fast-track in 1996 and also received two separate salary increases in response to competing job offers.

Albert Crenshaw

Albert Crenshaw was paid more than Hamilton on the 1992 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Crenshaw was paid more than Mayer on the 1995 to 1999 salary snapshots, similarly to Mayer on the 2000 salary snapshot and less than Mayer on the 2001 and 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Crenshaw came to The Post in the early 1970s as an Assistant Editor in National News. He became the Night Editor in National in 1974, the Assignment Editor in National in 1978 and became the Chief Copy Desk in National in 1981. In 1982, Crenshaw became the Editor of Real Estate, later becoming the Assistant Financial Editor in 1985. He became a reporter in Financial News in 1987. Prior to starting at The Post, Crenshaw worked as an Assistant City Editor at the Washington Daily News for approximately three-and-a-half years. Crenshaw is a graduate of Harvard University, and has a Masters in Journalism from Columbia and a Masters in Geology from the University of Virginia.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Crenshaw received approximately an 11 percent increase over his prior salary at the Washington Daily News. Hamilton and Mayer did not work at The Post at that time. When Hamilton started at The Post in 1972, Crenshaw was paid more than Hamilton at that time. When Mayer started at The Post in 1981, Crenshaw was paid substantially more than Mayer at that time.

documents.title: Guild survey responses on race and sex at The Post (two-column typewritten sheet)
documents.subject: Quoted responses by Post employees (by race, sex, and job title) to a newsroom survey on discrimination — white/black men, editors and reporters discussing hiring, promotion, favoritism and AME policies
documents.date: unknown (contemporary with bargaining-committee materials, likely late 1970s-1980s)
documents.notes: Typewritten two-column page; the section is cut off at the top (first heading only partially visible: '...hite male, Metro, Editor:'). Content thematically matches the 'Could it be that the Post discriminates?' newsletter page in this batch (DOC-006) but is not physically consecutive with it, so recorded as a separate document. Bottom of page is slightly cut off in the photo.

pages.transcript:
[Column 1; first heading partially cut off — reads '...hite male, Metro, Editor:']

hite male, Metro, Editor:
Three observations:
1) As a white, I am not scared of numerical goals for minorities. The best whites will still do all right.
2) At this and other papers, the problem seems less one of hiring than of advancement. There is a healthy number of women and blacks on the Metro assigning desk, but I suspect the paper would consider it a risk to make the Metro editor a woman or a black. It is harder yet to see either being appointed managing editor down the road. As a result, most blacks I know, here and elsewhere, feel very strongly that they work in an extremely white environment and privately despair of ever being recognized by top management.
3) At first glance, the negatives of a black affairs officer seems to far outweigh the positives. It's likely to polarize the newsroom more than hiring goals and in some aspects push minorities out of the mainstream into a very specialized channel.

White male, National/Financial/Investigations/Foreign, Editor:
I think the problem is most critical at policy-making levels. A look around the table at story conference meetings each day says a lot: no blacks, few women. Their voices need to be heard, louder and more frequently. I don't see intentional racism — but institutionally, whites stick together, and whites hold the most important positions.

Black male, Reporter:
I suspect this poll is a public relations ploy by The Post; nothing will come of it. Second, I fear that, at best, The Post will rush to hire a few more blacks. That would be a tragedy. The problem is not so much the numbers as how blacks already here are treated — they are treated badly or ignored.
If The Post treated its black and female employees more justly it would naturally have a reputation as a good place for the best black reporters to work. Look at how the N.Y. Times has blacks in key positions — the White House, deputy national editor, Chicago bureau chief, labor reporter, etc.
Blacks here also are excluded from the social events and source-making contacts that feed up white reporters. That should stop! The paper should show the State Dept, White House and others that they stand behind black reporters just as they stand behind white reporters.

Black male, section blank, job blank:
I feel strongly that the key question in the survey is No. 4, the one on favoritism. The other questions pale in significance by comparison to that one.
Favoritism is not only a factor in how people are treated — that is, their promotion — it is also an element in hiring. And the favoritism has an impact not only on blacks and women, the focus of this survey, but on older employees too.
Unless and until the favoritism aspect of newsroom personnel practice is dealt with, such questions as the hiring of an AME to deal specifically with blacks are totally meaningless. Ditto for quotas and goals.
Two other observations: I think the idea of conducting a survey is an honorable one. However, I also think it betrays the great distance, or gap, that has developed between top newsroom management and black newsroom personnel. With the black population being only 50, it would seem that there would be more personal and direct ways of measuring black frustration, satisfaction, or whatever; better ways than exit interviews.
I have had many personally and professionally satisfying deal-[cut off]
ings with the newsroom and company personnel executives. But I

[Column 2]
think someone needs to reconsider the wisdom of having a group of white, middle-aged men conduct personnel relations in a building that is highly diverse in age, color and sex.

Black male, Photo/News Art, Editor:
This survey only begins to touch the surface of problems at The Post. In that respect The Post is a microcosm of the problems that plague this society.
All steps taken should be toward creating a mission for The Post and setting about to eliminate the contradictions that exist within The Post, its operation, its observations, and its "journalism" from The "Journal." Then we can create a better world, for all.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Editor:
This is a well-intentioned but useless survey.
The problem is not racial bias but institutional arrogance and insensitivity that victimizes both whites and blacks. Blacks with their understandable racial sensitivity blame it on prejudice. Whites see it for what it is — myopic management that fails to make managers accountable for both the morale and performance of those under them.
Unless this larger issue is attacked, quotas, targets, based on race will only raise false hopes in some and irritate others.
Recruiting articulate, sensitive reporters who understand and care about this city will do far more for The Post inside and outside the building than the measure suggested in this poll.
Their race is the least important factor.

Black male, Photo/News Art, Reporter:
I feel that although hiring an AME to help with communication with blacks could be helpful, it would have to be combined with the hiring of more blacks on all levels and judging them on their talents for whatever the intended job may be. Too many times blacks and women must undergo a microscopic screening process when they apply for a job that white males are not subjected to.
The feeling in the black community is that one must be three times as good or talented as a white in order to be considered equal. This whole screening process can turn away a potential star employee whose talents may not readily be seen. The result is the loss of a hard working employee.
As far as judging the amount of racism at The Post, the newsroom in particular, such questions as the attitude of whites that they have superior skills compared to blacks. Once that cloak is removed from the eyes of whites that are in editor positions, quite a few things could change for blacks and also women because the same attitude is used against them (though to a lesser extent for white women).

White male, Metro, Reporter:
I favor more vigorous recruitment of blacks for news jobs at The Post, but oppose extraordinary efforts to promote once they're at work here. Promotion is zero-sum game: the advantage of one group is the disadvantage of another. The newsroom ought to be a free market of talent, with the cream (black or white) rising to the top.
If management wants to see more blacks in supervisory roles, let it achieve that goal by hiring more top-notch blacks in the first place — NOT by tilting things to their favor after they've arrived. The latter policy can only further polarize an already somewhat racially divided newsroom. The former harms no one; except hopeful job seekers, to whom The Post has no responsibility.
[bottom edge of page cut off in photo]

documents.title: 'Could it be that the Post discriminates?' — bargaining committee newsletter page with median-salary charts
documents.subject: Guild/Washington Bargaining Committee newsletter page arguing the Post discriminates by race and sex: dual pay, the Guild pay proposal, top-25 earners statistics, and bar charts of median salaries for Outside Sales and Copy Editors (white males vs white females) by hire-year cohort
documents.notes: Typewritten newsletter/leaf page with two pasted-in bar charts, signed '-- Martha Hamilton, for the Bargaining Committee'. Thematically connected to DOC-003 (same survey/discussion material) but photographed separately; recorded as its own document. Charts: Y axes labeled MEDIAN SALARIES ($600-$1,000 for Outside Sales; $0-$1,000 for Copy Editors), X axes labeled HIRED with cohorts 60-64, 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84 (and 85+ for Copy Editors); legend pairs WHITE MALES (solid) vs WHITE FEMALES (hatched).

pages.transcript:
Could it be that the Post discriminates?

Post management says no. Post management says, in effect, that if women and blacks are good enough — and old enough and experienced enough, they will command the same salaries as white males. (Publisher Graham asserted to a bargaining committee member that minorities command premiums, although the data don't seem to bear that out.) If so, should we conclude that women and blacks who are not commanding comparable salaries are not good enough? Are the many white males who also suffer from an unfair and arbitrary salary system also failing to measure up?

We don't buy that. We don't think management can get by with blaming the victims.

The culprit is dual pay, which keeps minimums so low that the subjective decisions made in setting salaries and awarding merit increases are allowed to carve out a discriminatory pattern. The Guild's pay proposal, which would phase out dual pay at the top of the scale over three years, would reduce the gaps in pay based on race and sex considerably by the end of this contract. Handing out merit pay increases won't do it. Father knows best won't do it.

Equal pay for equal work will.

Still with us?

Of the top 25 earners in the newsroom, one is black and two are female. That's 88 percent white males. Of the top 100, seven are black and 13 are female. And, just in case you wondered, there is no overlap: there are no black women in the top 25 or the top 100. The median age of this group is 43. In other words, half of the group is 43 or younger, so it's not just venerable white men, either.

We have focused on reporters because reporters are the largest group of workers in the Guild unit and also because more merit pay is dished out in the newsroom, so salaries there reflect management discretion more than in some other areas of the newspaper.

[Chart:] OUTSIDE SALES
Y axis: MEDIAN SALARIES ($600 to $1,000). Legend: WHITE MALES (solid bars), WHITE FEMALES (hatched bars). X axis: HIRED — cohorts 60-64, 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84. Each cohort shows a taller white-male bar and a shorter white-female bar (gaps widening for the 60-64 and 75-79/80-84 cohorts; values roughly $920/$840, $870/$730, $880/$730, $790/$800, $780/$700 respectively — approximate from chart).

[Chart:] COPY EDITORS
Y axis: MEDIAN SALARIES ($0 to $1,000). Legend: WHITE MALES, WHITE FEMALES. X axis: HIRED — cohorts 60-64, 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85+. White-male bars consistently at or above white-female bars (near parity in 60-64 through 70-74 at about $1,000/$990, $960/$950, $960/$950; then $900/$880, $850/$790, $780/$750 approximately — read from chart).

The charts above show the median salaries for different groups of employes. We have chosen two of the larger categories and also categories where the number of women and minorities hired is large enough to illustrate whether or not there are disparities in pay. Although there are some deviations from the pattern, by and large white males seem to be better paid than women or blacks hired during the same time frame. But another pattern is clear, too: Dual pay is driving most salaries down.

-- Martha Hamilton, for the
Bargaining Committee
